evaluated.name: CheapImprovingProfitability
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Value stocks whose operating profitability has been trending up over five years are cheap because expectations are anchored to stale weak fundamentals; the combination of low price and improving returns on assets marks expectation errors that resolve as the improvement becomes undeniable.
evaluated.reasoning: Here profitability enters as a dynamic state (slope of ROA) rather than a level, so the interaction identifies value traps versus recovering value instead of restating static quality. The multiplicative rank form ensures only cheap-and-improving firms score high, separating them from expensive turnarounds and cheap deteriorating firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExpensiveWeakMarginGlamour
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(oiadp, sale), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The short side of the profitability-value interaction is the sharper one: firms trading at high price-to-sales multiples while sustaining weak operating margins embed growth and margin-expansion expectations that their historical economics do not support, and they underperform as those expectations are revised down.
evaluated.reasoning: Price-to-sales is a valuation measure that is uninformative on its own because it mixes cheapness with margin structure; interacting it with realized three-year margins supplies the missing normalization and identifies genuinely overpriced firms. Deliberately targeting the expensive-plus-unprofitable corner tests whether the interaction's alpha is concentrated in the short leg rather than merely mirroring signal 1.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkValueQuality
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only firms that clear a high bar on both dimensions at once — durable operating profitability and a depressed price relative to book capital — represent fundamentals-versus-expectations mismatches; a firm that fails either test should be scored by its failing dimension, not compensated by strength elsewhere.
evaluated.reasoning: MIN is a strict conjunction and is not spanned by the average of the two ranks: unlike the product or the sum, it refuses to let extreme cheapness offset weak profitability (or vice versa), so its cross-sectional variation is orthogonal to an additive quality-plus-value composite in exactly the region where the two themes conflict. Using operating profitability scaled by assets rather than gross profits, and industry-relative ranks, keeps the profitability leg comparable across capital structures while the conjunction form supplies the genuine interaction content.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitTiltedCashYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-earnings yield should be rewarded when sustained operating profitability is above the industry norm and actively penalized when it is below, because a high yield on chronically weak economics reflects melting earnings and distress rather than undervaluation.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the degenerate 0/1 gate with a signed, continuous industry z-score removes the mass point and the perverse ordering: cheap-and-profitable firms score most positive, cheap-and-unprofitable firms score most negative, and firms with industry-average profitability sit in the middle regardless of yield. Ranking the valuation leg makes it robust to negative and fat-tailed earnings yields, so the sign flip comes only from the profitability channel, which is the economic content of the interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryProfitValuationGap
evaluated.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose return on assets is near its own five-year high while its price-to-book multiple sits near its own five-year low is being repriced downward exactly when its economics are strongest, and this within-firm contradiction between fundamental state and market-assigned multiple is resolved by subsequent outperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: The comparison is time-series rather than cross-sectional, so it cannot collapse into an equal-weighted cross-sectional value-plus-profitability composite: a permanently low-multiple, permanently low-margin firm scores zero, whereas the cross-sectional composite would rate it cheap. It therefore isolates changes in the market's willingness to pay for a firm's own fundamentals, holding fixed the firm's structural level of profitability and typical multiple.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DeepValueTrapScreen
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within the cheapest tercile on operating cash flow to price, the spread between operationally profitable firms and value traps is the dominant source of return dispersion; expensive firms carry no reliable signal and should be held neutral rather than shorted.
evaluated.reasoning: The gate is placed on the valuation leg and the graded score on the profitability leg, so the neutral (zero) group sits naturally at the center of a mean-zero industry z-score instead of being ranked above profitable firms, curing the breakpoint pathology of the earlier version. Cash-flow-to-price avoids the negative and near-zero enterprise-value outliers of a GP/EV construction, and operating profitability net of overhead (revt − cogs − xsga) is the discriminator most likely to separate genuine cheapness from decaying businesses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithDebtServiceCapacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), xint))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is ambiguous because it mixes mispricing with default risk; among value stocks, the firms whose operating profits comfortably cover total debt and interest are undervalued, while those whose profits cannot service their obligations are correctly cheap and keep underperforming.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs of the spread live inside the top-40% book-to-market group, so HML exposure largely cancels and the surviving variation is profit-based solvency, which RMW does not capture because it ignores the liability side. Using ceq/ME rather than oancf/ME for the gate roughly doubles usable coverage relative to DeepValueTrapScreen while keeping the same alpha-preserving geometry.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: GlamourProfitDeterioration
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(DELTA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: High-multiple firms are priced on continued margin expansion, so within the expensive group the firms whose return on assets is already falling face the largest expectation revisions, while expensive firms with still-improving profitability justify their multiples.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the deliberate mirror of Signal 3 with the valuation state fixed at the opposite extreme, so the pair identifies whether the profitability-value interaction is generated on the cheap side, the expensive side, or both — information no single-gate signal can provide. Because both legs are expensive stocks, the spread is again close to HML-neutral, isolating the interaction rather than the value effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithStableProfits
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(VOL(RATIO(oibdp, at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors discount value stocks as a group for fundamental uncertainty, but the discount is applied indiscriminately: cheap firms whose operating profitability has been quiet and stable over five years carry far less genuine cash-flow risk than the cheap firms with erratic profits, so the stable ones are systematically over-discounted.
evaluated.reasoning: The graded channel is a second moment of profitability, not its level or its accrual composition, so it is neither Sloan accruals nor anything RMW measures — FF5 has no factor for profit-stream volatility. Because both legs sit inside the top-40% book-to-market group, HML exposure nets out and the surviving spread is the risk-versus-mispricing distinction inside value, which is exactly the geometry that produced FF5 alpha in gen 0.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: QualityDeratedVersusOwnHistory
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Durably profitable firms rarely become cheap in the cross-section, so their mispricing shows up as de-rating relative to their own valuation history: a high-profitability firm trading at the bottom of its own five-year price-to-book range has been repriced without a corresponding deterioration in its economics, and that gap closes.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the trivial cross-sectional value leg with a within-firm valuation position, which is close to orthogonal to HML because a structurally expensive quality firm at its own five-year low can still be an expensive stock cross-sectionally. Gating on three-year average operating profitability keeps both legs inside the high-quality group, so RMW nets out too, leaving a de-rating-of-quality spread that no FF5 factor represents.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EnterpriseYieldGateOperatingProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity-only cheapness confounds genuine undervaluation with financial leverage, so defining cheapness as operating earnings relative to total capitalization identifies firms whose whole enterprise is discounted; within that group, high operating profitability marks the ones whose discount is unwarranted.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice relative to Signal 1 — whether debt belongs in the valuation denominator — and directly tests whether the levered value traps that plague equity-based cheapness were diluting the earlier gates. Adding debt rather than subtracting cash keeps the denominator strictly positive, avoiding the sign-flipping enterprise-value outliers the critic flagged in gen 0.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithOverheadEfficiency
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within firms cheap on cash-flow yield, the decisive fundamental is how much gross profit the business extracts per dollar of overhead spending: high gross-profit-to-SG&A firms have scalable, self-funding operations, while cheap firms that must spend heavily on selling and administration to sustain the same gross profit are structurally declining and deservedly discounted.
evaluated.reasoning: This keeps DeepValueTrapScreen's gate variable and threshold exactly unchanged and alters only the grading channel, so it is a clean one-factor experiment rather than the cosmetic proxy-plus-threshold swap the critic rejected. Gross profit per dollar of overhead is an efficiency ratio with a strictly positive denominator, is not a scaled-profit measure of the RMW type, and therefore has a real chance of producing a within-value spread that FF5 cannot absorb.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashYieldGateProfitPersistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), 0.5), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms cheap on cash-flow yield, undervaluation is distinguished from decline by how many of the past five years the firm ranked in the upper half of its industry on operating return on assets; repeated competitive standing shows the depressed price reflects sentiment rather than a broken business model.
evaluated.reasoning: The threshold is now applied to a cross-sectional industry rank at the median, matching the archive's INDICATOR convention, so the yearly flag splits the sample roughly in half and the five-year sum spans 0 to 5 with genuine dispersion instead of collapsing to a constant. Holding the winner's gate fixed makes this a direct level-versus-persistence test of what generated the only FF5 alpha in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueCheapMarginExpansion
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms priced cheaply per dollar of revenue are valued as if their thin margins are permanent; when the gross margin of such a firm actually widens, the revenue base is being repriced upward in economic terms long before the market re-rates the multiple, whereas revenue-cheap firms with contracting margins are in genuine competitive decline.
evaluated.reasoning: Grading on the *change* in gross margin rather than its level breaks the critic's E/P equivalence, because a high-scoring firm here can still have low current earnings yield — what matters is the direction of the margin, not its size. The construction targets exactly the operating-leverage repricing that revenue-based cheapness makes possible and uses a ratio bounded between 0 and 1 whose first difference is numerically well behaved.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SustainableDividendValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dvc, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the market pricing in a cut; among high-yield firms, those whose dividend consumes only a small fraction of gross profit have ample cushion and will sustain the payout, while those distributing a large share of gross profit are the ones whose yield is a warning rather than a bargain.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling the dividend by gross profit rather than by assets makes the grading term a true payout-coverage measure with dividends in the numerator, fixing the critic's point that (oiadp − dvc)/at was numerically just ROA. Gross profit is positive for essentially all firms, so unlike a dvc/oibdp coverage ratio this construction cannot award top scores to loss-making payers through a sign flip.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithLowCapitalConsumption
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: For asset-heavy value firms most of the gross profit is silently consumed by capital replacement, so within the cheap group the firms whose depreciation absorbs a small share of gross profit generate genuinely distributable earnings, while those with heavy capital consumption must reinvest merely to stand still and their book value overstates recoverable capital.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing operating profit with gross profit in the denominator removes the sign flip that would have handed top scores to loss-making cheap firms, since revt − cogs is positive for virtually the entire gated sample, while the economic content — capital intensity of profit generation — is unchanged. That channel is distinct from RMW's margin definition and from CMA's asset-growth definition, so a within-value spread on it is a genuine candidate for surviving FF5.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ConsolidatedCheapEarningPowerBurden
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), 0.5), 5), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms cheap per dollar of gross profit, two independent things determine whether the discount is unjustified: whether the firm has repeatedly held an above-median competitive return on assets, and whether its gross profit is free of heavy capital-replacement claims; firms strong on both are the genuine mispricings.
evaluated.reasoning: This deliberately fuses the one channel that produced FMB significance (profit persistence, fmb 2.7) with the one that produced the most reliable FF5 alpha (low burden on gross profit, t 2.2-3.6), which are near-orthogonal statistics — a five-year competitive-standing count and a current capital-intensity ratio. Using gross profit to price as the gate raises coverage well above the oancf-gated winners while keeping the alpha-preserving property that both legs sit inside the cheap group.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithUnpledgedGrossProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(xint, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms differ sharply in how much of their gross profit is already promised to lenders; when interest consumes little of gross profit the equity holder captures the recovery in a discounted business, whereas when interest absorbs a large share the equity is a residual claim on a levered, correctly discounted firm.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the correct repair of gen 1's CheapWithDebtServiceCapacity, whose FMB slope flipped to −1.4 precisely because oibdp/(debt+interest) explodes for near-zero-leverage firms; here the unstable quantity is placed in the numerator and divided by gross profit, which is positive for nearly every firm. It also tests whether Family B generalizes across burden types — dividends, depreciation, and now interest — or whether the two successes were channel-specific.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetCashValueWithProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oiadp, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a large fraction of market capitalization is covered by net cash on the balance sheet, the operating business is being valued at close to nothing; that is a bargain only if the operating business actually earns a return, because for a loss-maker the cash is a burn reserve rather than a store of value.
evaluated.reasoning: The valuation channel is balance-sheet liquidity value rather than any earnings- or book-based multiple, so its long-short spread is structurally different from HML and from every gate used so far in the archive. The interaction is essential rather than decorative: net-cash cheapness is famously contaminated by cash-burning firms, and profitability is exactly the variable that separates the two interpretations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DividendCoverageWithEarningPower
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dvc, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)), RATIO(oiadp, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the market forecasting a cut, and two conditions refute that forecast jointly: the dividend absorbs only a small share of gross profit, and the underlying assets still earn a solid operating return; a payout that is cheap to fund out of a productive asset base will be maintained.
evaluated.reasoning: SustainableDividendValue produced the archive's most reliable alpha (t 3.6) with a flat FMB slope, which suggests the coverage ratio orders the extreme portfolios well but is a weak linear predictor on its own; adding an operating-profitability rank inside the same gate supplies the cross-sectional slope that channel lacks. This is a targeted diagnosis-driven fix, not a variant: it tests whether coverage and earning power are complements within the yield-gated universe.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapDeleveragingFromProfits
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a cheap firm devotes a meaningful share of its gross profit to retiring debt, value is transferred from creditors to equity holders while the equity multiple stays anchored to the pre-deleveraging risk perception; cheap firms that are instead adding debt relative to their profit base are financing decline and their discount is warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the rejected operator swap with a new economic channel — capital-structure dynamics financed out of profits — that no archive signal touches, and it explains why value equities re-rate slowly: the equity claim's risk falls before the multiple responds. Scaling the change in debt by gross profit rather than by assets makes the measure an intensity of profit deployment with a strictly positive denominator, avoiding the sign instability that broke the gen-1 debt-coverage signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithTaxValidatedProfits
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(pi, ib), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash taxes are the most costly and therefore most credible confirmation that a value firm's reported profits are economically real; among cheap firms, those paying a substantial tax charge relative to gross profit have earnings validated by an outside authority, while those reporting profits with negligible tax expense are relying on accounting constructs or carried-forward losses that signal a genuinely impaired business.
evaluated.reasoning: The grading channel is the tax wedge between pretax and after-tax income — an earnings-credibility measure entirely absent from FF5, from RMW's margin definition, and from the archive, so it is not the R&D-to-market anomaly the critic rejected nor an accruals restatement. Deflating the tax charge by gross profit keeps the denominator positive for essentially all firms and avoids the COALESCE mass point, so the signal varies continuously across the whole gated universe rather than splitting reporters from non-reporters.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EquityShareOfGrossProfitValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), xint), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two cheap firms with identical gross profit are worth very different amounts depending on how much of that profit must be surrendered to maintain the asset base and service lenders; the share of gross profit still available to equity after capital consumption and interest is the true earning power behind the discount, and the market prices the discount without pricing the composition.
evaluated.reasoning: This unifies the two separately validated burden channels (dp/gross profit at t 2.24 and xint/gross profit at t 2.81) into one economically interpretable quantity — equity's residual claim on gross profit — rather than averaging their ranks, so the composite is a single ratio with no discrete leg to dominate it. Both numerator components are deductions from the same positive denominator, so the measure is bounded in practice and free of the sign flips that broke earlier coverage ratios.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ClaimShareAndDebtFlowValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The stock of claims on gross profit and the direction in which those claims are moving are complementary pieces of information: a cheap firm with little of its profit pre-committed and which is additionally retiring debt out of that profit is transferring value to equity on both dimensions at once.
evaluated.reasoning: This fuses the archive's only signal strong on both metrics (CheapDeleveragingFromProfits, fmb 4.75 and alpha t 2.14) with the burden-level channel that supplies reliable alpha, and unlike gen 3's failed fusion both legs are continuous ratios sharing the same gross-profit denominator, so neither can dominate the ordering through discreteness. The economic content is the level and the flow of the same quantity, which is why averaging their ranks is coherent rather than arbitrary.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: GlamourWithEncumberedProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms are priced on the assumption that reported profit will be reinvested into growth; when a large share of gross profit is instead absorbed by depreciation and interest, that growth is unfinanceable from internal resources and the high multiple is unsustainable.
evaluated.reasoning: This locates the mechanism by running the validated burden channel inside the opposite valuation state, so a strong negative alpha would show the claim-share effect is general to expectations while a null would show it is specific to distressed-price firms. It costs one slot to answer a question that no amount of refinement within the cheap gate can settle, and it uses the identical grading construction so the comparison is clean.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetCashCheapUnencumberedProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When net cash covers much of market capitalization the operating business is nearly free, and the business is worth having only if its gross profit is not consumed by capital replacement; cash-rich firms whose operations devour their own profit are burning the very reserve that makes them look cheap.
evaluated.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two most distinct successes — the net-cash valuation gate that produced an FMB slope of 2.58 and the capital-consumption channel that produced reliable alpha — since each supplies the form of evidence the other lacks. It also addresses the critic's concern that the net-cash long leg concentrates in cash-burning microcaps, because the grading channel explicitly ranks those firms at the bottom.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AfterTaxEquityShareOfGrossProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), xint), SUB(pi, ib)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The claims that genuinely reduce what equity can compound are the mandatory payments to outside parties — physical capital replacement, lenders, and the tax authority — and among cheap firms the fraction of gross profit surviving all three is the real distributable earning power behind the discount.
evaluated.reasoning: Dividends are removed because they accrue to the equity holder rather than to an outside claimant, which was the incoherent element of the previous aggregate; what remains is a prior-based definition of non-equity claims rather than a sign-fitted sum. Relative to the accepted EquityShareOfGrossProfitValue this changes exactly one term — the tax wedge — so it cleanly answers whether the fiscal claim carries information beyond the operating and financing claims.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkCheapUnencumberedProfit
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is an attractive profitable-value proposition only if it clears a high bar on both dimensions simultaneously — a depressed price relative to book and gross profit that is not consumed by capital replacement — and failing either dimension should determine the score, because deep cheapness cannot compensate for profit that never reaches equity.
evaluated.reasoning: This preserves the interaction mandate the univariate yield abandoned while still removing the 60% mass point at zero that has flattened every gated signal's Fama-MacBeth slope, since MIN is continuous over the whole cross-section and is a strict conjunction not spanned by the average of its two ranks. Gen 0's MIN construction achieved fmb 4.15 but negative alpha because its second leg was RMW-like asset-scaled profitability; substituting the capital-consumption share, which the archive shows is FF5-orthogonal, targets both metrics at once.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapProfitFundedDisgorgement
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(dvc, 0), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm that uses its gross profit to hand cash out — paying dividends while simultaneously retiring debt — is demonstrating that the profit is real, unencumbered and under disciplined management, whereas a cheap firm absorbing new debt while distributing nothing is consuming outside capital to sustain itself and its discount is warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: This generalizes the archive's only two-metric success from debt repayment alone to total profit-funded disgorgement to all capital providers, which is the same economic flow measured more completely, and it keeps dividends in their coherent role as a distribution to equity rather than as a "burden". The flow construction is what supplied the FMB slope of 4.75, so the extension targets both metrics rather than adding another static claim-level ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapClaimsPerRevenueDollar
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economic content of the claim-share mechanism is how heavily capital replacement and interest weigh on the business's scale of operations, and revenue is the correct scale measure because it is always positive; cheap firms carrying light fixed claims per dollar of revenue retain the flexibility to survive and re-rate.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the repair of the defect the critic identified across the whole burden family: with gross profit in the denominator, a firm with negative gross profit receives a spuriously *favorable* score, and such firms are common in the cheap gate, so part of the archived alphas may be driven by an inverted subsample. Substituting sales removes the inversion entirely while leaving the mechanism intact, so a comparison against EquityShareOfGrossProfitValue tells us how much of that alpha was real.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HighYieldGateUnencumberedProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), ADD(dp, xint)), sale), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The market treats a high dividend yield as a forecast of a cut; that forecast is refuted when the firm's revenue base carries light capital-replacement and interest claims, because such a firm can fund the payout out of ordinary operations without borrowing or underinvesting.
evaluated.reasoning: The dividend-yield gate has produced the archive's two most reliable alphas (t 3.62 and t 4.14), and this pairs it for the first time with the unified claim measure rather than with a payout ratio or an asset-scaled profitability rank, so it tests whether the yield gate's power comes from payout safety specifically or from unencumbered earning power generally. Revenue scaling keeps the grading leg free of the negative-gross-profit inversion, and coverage stays at the archive's high end because only dividends, price and income-statement items are needed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapUnencumberedAndGrowing
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2)), GROWTH(SUB(revt, cogs), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm re-rates when its profit base is both lightly encumbered and actually expanding: light capital-replacement and interest claims mean growth can be self-funded, and observed gross-profit growth shows the business is winning rather than merely surviving, so the two conditions together identify discounts that the market will be forced to retract.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces horizon tuning with new economic content — the archive has tested claim *levels* and claim *flows* but never whether the encumbrance mechanism requires an expanding profit base — and it targets the one diagnostic that has failed everywhere in the archive, the near-zero long-short Sharpe, since a growing profit base should lift raw returns rather than only factor-adjusted ones. Both legs use a strictly positive revenue scale, avoiding the negative-gross-profit inversion.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapSelfFundedEquityBase
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), ib), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), sale), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book equity grows only through retained earnings or through external injection, so the residual after subtracting earnings and adding back dividends measures how much outside equity capital a firm consumed; among firms cheap on operating earnings, those funding themselves entirely from profits are undervalued, while those repeatedly absorbing outside equity at a low price are transferring value away from existing holders.
evaluated.reasoning: The clean-surplus residual is immune to the splits and stock dividends that contaminate raw share-count changes, which was the mechanical flaw in the previous version, and scaling by revenue removes the sign inversion of a gross-profit denominator. It is not the net-stock-issuance anomaly: the measure is a balance-sheet financing intensity relative to operating scale, evaluated only inside a cheapness gate defined on operating earnings, so it captures the reliance on outside capital rather than the issuance event itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapEquityDearToCreditors
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(xint, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity and credit markets can disagree about the same firm: when the equity market demands a high operating earnings yield while the firm's own lenders accept a low interest rate, the better-informed creditors are contradicting the equity market's risk assessment, and the equity discount is the side that corrects.
evaluated.reasoning: Making the equity-market leg a gate rather than a subtracted term removes the arithmetic problem the critic identified — E/P dispersion swamping the borrowing-rate term — so the cross-sectional spread is generated entirely by the creditor-implied rate within a cheap universe, and the signal cannot collapse into plain E/P. Coverage is honestly limited to firms with debt outstanding, which is the economically correct domain because a firm with no borrowings has no creditor opinion to compare against.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithImprovingCreditTerms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xint, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Lenders reprice a firm's risk before equity investors do, so a falling effective interest rate on a firm that is still cheap on operating earnings is the credit market's verdict that the risk has receded while the equity discount persists.
evaluated.reasoning: The level version of this cross-market comparison already worked (CheapEquityDearToCreditors: fmb 2.15, alpha 2.6%, t 2.00), and the archive's clearest lesson is that flows carry the cross-sectional slope while levels do not, so converting the creditor signal from a level to a change is exactly the transformation that has repeatedly raised fmb from ~2 to >4. Coverage is properly confined to firms with debt outstanding, since only they have a creditor-set price.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapWithLongDatedObligations
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm re-rates only if it survives long enough to do so, and survival depends less on how much debt it owes than on when that debt falls due; a high share of current maturities forces refinancing into exactly the weak market conditions that created the discount, while long-dated obligations buy the time for operating profit to be recognized.
evaluated.reasoning: Every claim measure in the archive concerns the size of obligations; this one concerns their timing, which is a genuinely new channel and one that FF5 cannot represent since neither HML nor RMW nor CMA contains maturity information. The ratio is bounded between zero and one by construction, so it needs no denominator repair and produces a stable, well-behaved cross-sectional spread inside the cheapness gate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapNetCashAccretion
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), sale), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The clearest evidence that a cheap firm's operations generate real surplus is the annual rate at which its net financial position improves — cash accumulating faster than borrowings — because that improvement can only come from operations, and it steadily converts a levered, risky equity claim into a safe one while the discount persists.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the external-financing measure repackaged: a firm can raise no capital and repay no debt yet still accrete net cash, and conversely a firm can repay debt by drawing down cash with no change in net position, so the two constructions rank firms differently in exactly the cases that matter. It keeps the sales deflator that demonstrably improved slope and Sharpe, and it uses balance-sheet stocks rather than a dollar sum of the two archived flow legs.

evaluated.name: CheapBurdenAtOwnHistoricalLow
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: How heavy a firm's fixed claims are cannot be judged against other firms, because capital intensity is a permanent feature of a business model; what signals genuine improvement is a claim burden sitting at the low end of the firm's own five-year range, which means the firm has been de-risked relative to the operating history the market is still discounting.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a cross-sectional level with a within-firm position statistic, which is a different kind of measurement rather than a different deflator, and it removes the confound that made the archived level channels slope-dead — permanent industry differences in depreciation and leverage intensity dominate the cross-section but cancel entirely in a firm's own history. It preserves the flow-like informativeness that has driven every strong Fama-MacBeth slope in the archive while retaining the level channel's alpha-bearing content.

evaluated.name: CheapClaimsMeetStableProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2), WINSOR(VOL(RATIO(oibdp, sale), 5), 2)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fixed claims are dangerous only in proportion to the variability of the profit that must cover them; a cheap firm with heavy capital-replacement and interest obligations and an erratic margin faces genuine ruin risk, whereas the same obligations against a stable margin are simply a financing arrangement and do not justify a discount.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive tested claim size (alpha 2.5%, dead slope) and profit stability (fmb 3.73, dead alpha) as separate additive channels; this multiplies them, which is the economically correct combination for a solvency risk that is the product of exposure and volatility, and it is the first construction that could inherit the slope from one channel and the alpha from the other. It replaces the flagged glamour mirror with a mechanism that FF5 cannot represent, since no factor contains a second moment of profitability.

evaluated.name: CheapWithOverheadRestructuring
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xsga, sale), 1), 2))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms are cheap because the market expects their cost base to overwhelm their revenue; when overhead per dollar of sales actually falls, management has demonstrated it can restructure, and the operating leverage released flows to equity before analysts revise their fixed-cost assumptions.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves the flow concept from the financing side of the firm — where the critic correctly notes the published issuance and external-finance literature already lives — to the operating cost side, which no archive signal has tested as a change. evaluated.name: CheapChronicSelfFunding

evaluated.hypothesis: What distinguishes a mispriced cheap firm from a value trap is not whether it avoided outside capital last year but whether it has done so repeatedly: a firm that has generated earnings in excess of its capital growth in most of the past five years has a business model that funds itself, whereas an occasional good year tells the market nothing.
evaluated.reasoning: This applies a persistence statistic — which is the one construction that delivered both metrics for profitability (fmb 2.71, alpha 2.8%) — to the flow quantity that now dominates the archive's slopes (fmb 4.5-4.8), so it is a new statistic on a validated channel rather than another dollar-sum repackaging. Free capital generation is defined as one accounting quantity, earnings minus the growth in total invested capital, and the yearly flag is an industry-relative median rank so the five-year count spans 0 to 5 with real dispersion.

evaluated.name: CheapSelfFundedDistributableProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), ADD(dp, xint)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), sale), 2)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The profit an equity holder in a cheap firm can actually count on is gross profit less what capital replacement and lenders take, less whatever new borrowing was required to keep the business running; when that residual is large relative to revenue, the discount is unjustified regardless of how the accounting earnings look.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's two previous level-plus-flow fusions diluted (alpha 1.3% and 0.9%) because they averaged the *ranks* of two channels, letting each leg's noise offset the other; here the level and the flow are combined inside one accounting expression, so the composite is a single economic quantity — self-funded distributable profit — with one positive deflator. evaluated.name: CheapPayoutPerOperatingCost

evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, cash paid to shareholders net of new borrowing measures genuine surplus, and the right scale for that surplus is the firm's operating cost base — the recurring outlay the business must fund each year — because that is what determines whether the surplus is material to the enterprise.

evaluated.name: CheapLeveredWithNearTermMaturities

evaluated.hypothesis: Holding the amount of debt fixed, the share of it that matures within the year determines whether a cheap firm controls its own timetable; those funded long can let operating profit be recognized, while those with a large current tranche must refinance into the same adverse conditions that produced the discount.
evaluated.reasoning: The graded leg is now the pure maturity share, which contains no information about the size of borrowings, and the second indicator restricts scoring to firms above the 30th percentile of leverage so that companies with trivial debt balances — whose all-current micro-balances produced the instability the critic identified — are held at neutral rather than scored as maximum risk. evaluated.hypothesis: The complete measure of what a cheap firm returns to its capital providers is earnings less the growth in book equity — which captures dividends and repurchases together while netting out equity issuance — less any increase in debt; when that total is large, the firm is shrinking outside claims of every type out of current profit, and the equity holder's share compounds while the price stays depressed.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the published cash-holdings channel with the archive's most productive economic idea expressed completely: declared dividends alone (the archive's best signal) omit repurchases, which are the dominant distribution channel for most of the sample period, and the retained-earnings identity captures both without requiring split-contaminated share counts. It differs from the persistence version in Signal 1 of this batch by measuring current-year magnitude rather than frequency, so the two together separate how much from how often.

evaluated.name: LowReplacementValueDeleveraging

evaluated.hypothesis: The deepest form of undervaluation is an entire enterprise priced below the book cost of the assets it operates, and in that state the transfer of value from creditors to equity as debt is retired out of profit is the least visible to investors focused on the equity multiple alone.

evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, the cash actually delivered to shareholders — dividends plus repurchases net of any equity issued, which is exactly earnings minus the growth in book equity — is the credible signal that reported profit is real and surplus to the firm's needs, and the depressed price fails to capitalize it.

evaluated.name: TwoSidedCapitalReturnExpectations
evaluated.expression: MUL(SUB(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), 0.6)), IND_ZSCORE(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(ceq, 1)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga)), 2), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The mispricing is the disagreement between what price implies and what capital flows reveal: cheap firms that persistently return capital are stronger than their price admits, and expensive firms that persistently absorb outside capital are weaker than their price assumes, so the two corners belong in the same signal with opposite weights.
evaluated.reasoning: The state variable takes the values +1, 0 and −1 across the cheap, middle and expensive thirds and multiplies the capital-return z-score, so the score is highest for cheap disgorgers and lowest for expensive absorbers — which fixes the sign inconsistency of the previous version and, more importantly, makes the construction a true interaction term rather than a gated single-state effect. It is the one specification that tests the project's central claim directly, that profitability-type evidence flips its return implication with the valuation state instead of merely being layered onto it.

considered.name: CheapImprovingProfitability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Value stocks whose operating profitability has been trending up over five years are cheap because expectations are anchored to stale weak fundamentals; the combination of low price and improving returns on assets marks expectation errors that resolve as the improvement becomes undeniable.
considered.reasoning: Here profitability enters as a dynamic state (slope of ROA) rather than a level, so the interaction identifies value traps versus recovering value instead of restating static quality. The multiplicative rank form ensures only cheap-and-improving firms score high, separating them from expensive turnarounds and cheap deteriorating firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExpensiveWeakMarginGlamour
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(oiadp, sale), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: The short side of the profitability-value interaction is the sharper one: firms trading at high price-to-sales multiples while sustaining weak operating margins embed growth and margin-expansion expectations that their historical economics do not support, and they underperform as those expectations are revised down.
considered.reasoning: Price-to-sales is a valuation measure that is uninformative on its own because it mixes cheapness with margin structure; interacting it with realized three-year margins supplies the missing normalization and identifies genuinely overpriced firms. Deliberately targeting the expensive-plus-unprofitable corner tests whether the interaction's alpha is concentrated in the short leg rather than merely mirroring signal 1.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WeakestLinkValueQuality
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Only firms that clear a high bar on both dimensions at once — durable operating profitability and a depressed price relative to book capital — represent fundamentals-versus-expectations mismatches; a firm that fails either test should be scored by its failing dimension, not compensated by strength elsewhere.
considered.reasoning: MIN is a strict conjunction and is not spanned by the average of the two ranks: unlike the product or the sum, it refuses to let extreme cheapness offset weak profitability (or vice versa), so its cross-sectional variation is orthogonal to an additive quality-plus-value composite in exactly the region where the two themes conflict. Using operating profitability scaled by assets rather than gross profits, and industry-relative ranks, keeps the profitability leg comparable across capital structures while the conjunction form supplies the genuine interaction content.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitTiltedCashYield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash-earnings yield should be rewarded when sustained operating profitability is above the industry norm and actively penalized when it is below, because a high yield on chronically weak economics reflects melting earnings and distress rather than undervaluation.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the degenerate 0/1 gate with a signed, continuous industry z-score removes the mass point and the perverse ordering: cheap-and-profitable firms score most positive, cheap-and-unprofitable firms score most negative, and firms with industry-average profitability sit in the middle regardless of yield. Ranking the valuation leg makes it robust to negative and fat-tailed earnings yields, so the sign flip comes only from the profitability channel, which is the economic content of the interaction.

considered.name: OwnHistoryProfitValuationGap
considered.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose return on assets is near its own five-year high while its price-to-book multiple sits near its own five-year low is being repriced downward exactly when its economics are strongest, and this within-firm contradiction between fundamental state and market-assigned multiple is resolved by subsequent outperformance.
considered.reasoning: The comparison is time-series rather than cross-sectional, so it cannot collapse into an equal-weighted cross-sectional value-plus-profitability composite: a permanently low-multiple, permanently low-margin firm scores zero, whereas the cross-sectional composite would rate it cheap. It therefore isolates changes in the market's willingness to pay for a firm's own fundamentals, holding fixed the firm's structural level of profitability and typical multiple.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeepValueTrapScreen
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Within the cheapest tercile on operating cash flow to price, the spread between operationally profitable firms and value traps is the dominant source of return dispersion; expensive firms carry no reliable signal and should be held neutral rather than shorted.
considered.reasoning: The gate is placed on the valuation leg and the graded score on the profitability leg, so the neutral (zero) group sits naturally at the center of a mean-zero industry z-score instead of being ranked above profitable firms, curing the breakpoint pathology of the earlier version. Cash-flow-to-price avoids the negative and near-zero enterprise-value outliers of a GP/EV construction, and operating profitability net of overhead (revt − cogs − xsga) is the discriminator most likely to separate genuine cheapness from decaying businesses.

considered.name: CheapWithDebtServiceCapacity
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), xint))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness is ambiguous because it mixes mispricing with default risk; among value stocks, the firms whose operating profits comfortably cover total debt and interest are undervalued, while those whose profits cannot service their obligations are correctly cheap and keep underperforming.
considered.reasoning: Both legs of the spread live inside the top-40% book-to-market group, so HML exposure largely cancels and the surviving variation is profit-based solvency, which RMW does not capture because it ignores the liability side. Using ceq/ME rather than oancf/ME for the gate roughly doubles usable coverage relative to DeepValueTrapScreen while keeping the same alpha-preserving geometry.

considered.name: GlamourProfitDeterioration
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(DELTA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: High-multiple firms are priced on continued margin expansion, so within the expensive group the firms whose return on assets is already falling face the largest expectation revisions, while expensive firms with still-improving profitability justify their multiples.
considered.reasoning: This is the deliberate mirror of Signal 3 with the valuation state fixed at the opposite extreme, so the pair identifies whether the profitability-value interaction is generated on the cheap side, the expensive side, or both — information no single-gate signal can provide. Because both legs are expensive stocks, the spread is again close to HML-neutral, isolating the interaction rather than the value effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithStableProfits
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(VOL(RATIO(oibdp, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Investors discount value stocks as a group for fundamental uncertainty, but the discount is applied indiscriminately: cheap firms whose operating profitability has been quiet and stable over five years carry far less genuine cash-flow risk than the cheap firms with erratic profits, so the stable ones are systematically over-discounted.
considered.reasoning: The graded channel is a second moment of profitability, not its level or its accrual composition, so it is neither Sloan accruals nor anything RMW measures — FF5 has no factor for profit-stream volatility. Because both legs sit inside the top-40% book-to-market group, HML exposure nets out and the surviving spread is the risk-versus-mispricing distinction inside value, which is exactly the geometry that produced FF5 alpha in gen 0.

considered.name: CheapWithProductiveCapital
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(revt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: A low price relative to book equity is only informative if the book assets are still economically productive; among cheap firms, those that turn each dollar of assets into high sales own working capacity the market is valuing as scrap, whereas low-turnover cheap firms hold stranded assets whose book value overstates recoverable value.
considered.reasoning: Asset turnover is the capital-productivity limb of the DuPont decomposition and is essentially uncorrelated with the margin-based operating profitability that defines RMW, so the within-value spread it generates cannot be absorbed by either RMW or HML. It also replaces the flagged one-year ΔROA screen with a level-of-efficiency mechanism that is not a Piotroski F-score component, and it uses only revt and at, keeping coverage at the top of the archive rather than sacrificing it to a five-year window.

considered.name: QualityDeratedVersusOwnHistory
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Durably profitable firms rarely become cheap in the cross-section, so their mispricing shows up as de-rating relative to their own valuation history: a high-profitability firm trading at the bottom of its own five-year price-to-book range has been repriced without a corresponding deterioration in its economics, and that gap closes.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the trivial cross-sectional value leg with a within-firm valuation position, which is close to orthogonal to HML because a structurally expensive quality firm at its own five-year low can still be an expensive stock cross-sectionally. Gating on three-year average operating profitability keeps both legs inside the high-quality group, so RMW nets out too, leaving a de-rating-of-quality spread that no FF5 factor represents.

considered.name: LongRunCashYieldNotImpaired
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(oancf, MA(oancf, 5)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The right valuation anchor for a cash-generating business is the cumulative cash it has actually produced, and firms priced cheaply against five years of aggregate operating cash flow are attractive only when the latest year's cash generation is at or above its own normal level; a cheap long-run cash multiple combined with currently impaired cash flow signals a permanent step-down, not a discount.
considered.reasoning: The valuation leg is a five-year cumulative cash-flow multiple rather than any book-based ratio, so it is far less correlated with HML's input than the R&D-adjusted book value the critic rejected, and the graded leg is a current-versus-normal cash deviation that RMW does not contain. Scaling the deviation by assets rather than dividing by the moving average avoids the sign-flipping blow-ups that arise when a firm's average cash flow is near zero.

considered.name: EnterpriseYieldGateOperatingProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Equity-only cheapness confounds genuine undervaluation with financial leverage, so defining cheapness as operating earnings relative to total capitalization identifies firms whose whole enterprise is discounted; within that group, high operating profitability marks the ones whose discount is unwarranted.
considered.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice relative to Signal 1 — whether debt belongs in the valuation denominator — and directly tests whether the levered value traps that plague equity-based cheapness were diluting the earlier gates. Adding debt rather than subtracting cash keeps the denominator strictly positive, avoiding the sign-flipping enterprise-value outliers the critic flagged in gen 0.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithOverheadEfficiency
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Within firms cheap on cash-flow yield, the decisive fundamental is how much gross profit the business extracts per dollar of overhead spending: high gross-profit-to-SG&A firms have scalable, self-funding operations, while cheap firms that must spend heavily on selling and administration to sustain the same gross profit are structurally declining and deservedly discounted.
considered.reasoning: This keeps DeepValueTrapScreen's gate variable and threshold exactly unchanged and alters only the grading channel, so it is a clean one-factor experiment rather than the cosmetic proxy-plus-threshold swap the critic rejected. Gross profit per dollar of overhead is an efficiency ratio with a strictly positive denominator, is not a scaled-profit measure of the RMW type, and therefore has a real chance of producing a within-value spread that FF5 cannot absorb.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYieldGateProfitPersistence
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), 0.5), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms cheap on cash-flow yield, undervaluation is distinguished from decline by how many of the past five years the firm ranked in the upper half of its industry on operating return on assets; repeated competitive standing shows the depressed price reflects sentiment rather than a broken business model.
considered.reasoning: The threshold is now applied to a cross-sectional industry rank at the median, matching the archive's INDICATOR convention, so the yearly flag splits the sample roughly in half and the five-year sum spans 0 to 5 with genuine dispersion instead of collapsing to a constant. Holding the winner's gate fixed makes this a direct level-versus-persistence test of what generated the only FF5 alpha in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RevenueCheapMarginExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms priced cheaply per dollar of revenue are valued as if their thin margins are permanent; when the gross margin of such a firm actually widens, the revenue base is being repriced upward in economic terms long before the market re-rates the multiple, whereas revenue-cheap firms with contracting margins are in genuine competitive decline.
considered.reasoning: Grading on the *change* in gross margin rather than its level breaks the critic's E/P equivalence, because a high-scoring firm here can still have low current earnings yield — what matters is the direction of the margin, not its size. The construction targets exactly the operating-leverage repricing that revenue-based cheapness makes possible and uses a ratio bounded between 0 and 1 whose first difference is numerically well behaved.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SustainableDividendValue
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dvc, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the market pricing in a cut; among high-yield firms, those whose dividend consumes only a small fraction of gross profit have ample cushion and will sustain the payout, while those distributing a large share of gross profit are the ones whose yield is a warning rather than a bargain.
considered.reasoning: Scaling the dividend by gross profit rather than by assets makes the grading term a true payout-coverage measure with dividends in the numerator, fixing the critic's point that (oiadp − dvc)/at was numerically just ROA. Gross profit is positive for essentially all firms, so unlike a dvc/oibdp coverage ratio this construction cannot award top scores to loss-making payers through a sign flip.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithLowCapitalConsumption
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: For asset-heavy value firms most of the gross profit is silently consumed by capital replacement, so within the cheap group the firms whose depreciation absorbs a small share of gross profit generate genuinely distributable earnings, while those with heavy capital consumption must reinvest merely to stand still and their book value overstates recoverable capital.
considered.reasoning: Replacing operating profit with gross profit in the denominator removes the sign flip that would have handed top scores to loss-making cheap firms, since revt − cogs is positive for virtually the entire gated sample, while the economic content — capital intensity of profit generation — is unchanged. That channel is distinct from RMW's margin definition and from CMA's asset-growth definition, so a within-value spread on it is a genuine candidate for surviving FF5.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ConsolidatedCheapEarningPowerBurden
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), 0.5), 5), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms cheap per dollar of gross profit, two independent things determine whether the discount is unjustified: whether the firm has repeatedly held an above-median competitive return on assets, and whether its gross profit is free of heavy capital-replacement claims; firms strong on both are the genuine mispricings.
considered.reasoning: This deliberately fuses the one channel that produced FMB significance (profit persistence, fmb 2.7) with the one that produced the most reliable FF5 alpha (low burden on gross profit, t 2.2-3.6), which are near-orthogonal statistics — a five-year competitive-standing count and a current capital-intensity ratio. Using gross profit to price as the gate raises coverage well above the oancf-gated winners while keeping the alpha-preserving property that both legs sit inside the cheap group.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithUnpledgedGrossProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(xint, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms differ sharply in how much of their gross profit is already promised to lenders; when interest consumes little of gross profit the equity holder captures the recovery in a discounted business, whereas when interest absorbs a large share the equity is a residual claim on a levered, correctly discounted firm.
considered.reasoning: This is the correct repair of gen 1's CheapWithDebtServiceCapacity, whose FMB slope flipped to −1.4 precisely because oibdp/(debt+interest) explodes for near-zero-leverage firms; here the unstable quantity is placed in the numerator and divided by gross profit, which is positive for nearly every firm. It also tests whether Family B generalizes across burden types — dividends, depreciation, and now interest — or whether the two successes were channel-specific.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetCashValueWithProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oiadp, at)))
considered.hypothesis: When a large fraction of market capitalization is covered by net cash on the balance sheet, the operating business is being valued at close to nothing; that is a bargain only if the operating business actually earns a return, because for a loss-maker the cash is a burn reserve rather than a store of value.
considered.reasoning: The valuation channel is balance-sheet liquidity value rather than any earnings- or book-based multiple, so its long-short spread is structurally different from HML and from every gate used so far in the archive. The interaction is essential rather than decorative: net-cash cheapness is famously contaminated by cash-burning firms, and profitability is exactly the variable that separates the two interpretations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DividendCoverageWithEarningPower
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dvc, SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)), RATIO(oiadp, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the market forecasting a cut, and two conditions refute that forecast jointly: the dividend absorbs only a small share of gross profit, and the underlying assets still earn a solid operating return; a payout that is cheap to fund out of a productive asset base will be maintained.
considered.reasoning: SustainableDividendValue produced the archive's most reliable alpha (t 3.6) with a flat FMB slope, which suggests the coverage ratio orders the extreme portfolios well but is a weak linear predictor on its own; adding an operating-profitability rank inside the same gate supplies the cross-sectional slope that channel lacks. This is a targeted diagnosis-driven fix, not a variant: it tests whether coverage and earning power are complements within the yield-gated universe.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapDeleveragingFromProfits
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: When a cheap firm devotes a meaningful share of its gross profit to retiring debt, value is transferred from creditors to equity holders while the equity multiple stays anchored to the pre-deleveraging risk perception; cheap firms that are instead adding debt relative to their profit base are financing decline and their discount is warranted.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the rejected operator swap with a new economic channel — capital-structure dynamics financed out of profits — that no archive signal touches, and it explains why value equities re-rate slowly: the equity claim's risk falls before the multiple responds. Scaling the change in debt by gross profit rather than by assets makes the measure an intensity of profit deployment with a strictly positive denominator, avoiding the sign instability that broke the gen-1 debt-coverage signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithTaxValidatedProfits
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(pi, ib), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash taxes are the most costly and therefore most credible confirmation that a value firm's reported profits are economically real; among cheap firms, those paying a substantial tax charge relative to gross profit have earnings validated by an outside authority, while those reporting profits with negligible tax expense are relying on accounting constructs or carried-forward losses that signal a genuinely impaired business.
considered.reasoning: The grading channel is the tax wedge between pretax and after-tax income — an earnings-credibility measure entirely absent from FF5, from RMW's margin definition, and from the archive, so it is not the R&D-to-market anomaly the critic rejected nor an accruals restatement. Deflating the tax charge by gross profit keeps the denominator positive for essentially all firms and avoids the COALESCE mass point, so the signal varies continuously across the whole gated universe rather than splitting reporters from non-reporters.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EquityShareOfGrossProfitValue
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), xint), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Two cheap firms with identical gross profit are worth very different amounts depending on how much of that profit must be surrendered to maintain the asset base and service lenders; the share of gross profit still available to equity after capital consumption and interest is the true earning power behind the discount, and the market prices the discount without pricing the composition.
considered.reasoning: This unifies the two separately validated burden channels (dp/gross profit at t 2.24 and xint/gross profit at t 2.81) into one economically interpretable quantity — equity's residual claim on gross profit — rather than averaging their ranks, so the composite is a single ratio with no discrete leg to dominate it. Both numerator components are deductions from the same positive denominator, so the measure is bounded in practice and free of the sign flips that broke earlier coverage ratios.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ClaimShareAndDebtFlowValue
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))))
considered.hypothesis: The stock of claims on gross profit and the direction in which those claims are moving are complementary pieces of information: a cheap firm with little of its profit pre-committed and which is additionally retiring debt out of that profit is transferring value to equity on both dimensions at once.
considered.reasoning: This fuses the archive's only signal strong on both metrics (CheapDeleveragingFromProfits, fmb 4.75 and alpha t 2.14) with the burden-level channel that supplies reliable alpha, and unlike gen 3's failed fusion both legs are continuous ratios sharing the same gross-profit denominator, so neither can dominate the ordering through discreteness. The economic content is the level and the flow of the same quantity, which is why averaging their ranks is coherent rather than arbitrary.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GlamourWithEncumberedProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms are priced on the assumption that reported profit will be reinvested into growth; when a large share of gross profit is instead absorbed by depreciation and interest, that growth is unfinanceable from internal resources and the high multiple is unsustainable.
considered.reasoning: This locates the mechanism by running the validated burden channel inside the opposite valuation state, so a strong negative alpha would show the claim-share effect is general to expectations while a null would show it is specific to distressed-price firms. It costs one slot to answer a question that no amount of refinement within the cheap gate can settle, and it uses the identical grading construction so the comparison is clean.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetCashCheapUnencumberedProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: When net cash covers much of market capitalization the operating business is nearly free, and the business is worth having only if its gross profit is not consumed by capital replacement; cash-rich firms whose operations devour their own profit are burning the very reserve that makes them look cheap.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two most distinct successes — the net-cash valuation gate that produced an FMB slope of 2.58 and the capital-consumption channel that produced reliable alpha — since each supplies the form of evidence the other lacks. It also addresses the critic's concern that the net-cash long leg concentrates in cash-burning microcaps, because the grading channel explicitly ranks those firms at the bottom.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AfterTaxEquityShareOfGrossProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), xint), SUB(pi, ib)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: The claims that genuinely reduce what equity can compound are the mandatory payments to outside parties — physical capital replacement, lenders, and the tax authority — and among cheap firms the fraction of gross profit surviving all three is the real distributable earning power behind the discount.
considered.reasoning: Dividends are removed because they accrue to the equity holder rather than to an outside claimant, which was the incoherent element of the previous aggregate; what remains is a prior-based definition of non-equity claims rather than a sign-fitted sum. Relative to the accepted EquityShareOfGrossProfitValue this changes exactly one term — the tax wedge — so it cleanly answers whether the fiscal claim carries information beyond the operating and financing claims.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WeakestLinkCheapUnencumberedProfit
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), dp), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is an attractive profitable-value proposition only if it clears a high bar on both dimensions simultaneously — a depressed price relative to book and gross profit that is not consumed by capital replacement — and failing either dimension should determine the score, because deep cheapness cannot compensate for profit that never reaches equity.

considered.name: CheapProfitFundedDisgorgement
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(dvc, 0), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 2)))

The flow construction is what supplied the FMB slope of 4.75, so the extension targets both metrics rather than adding another static claim-level ratio.

considered.name: CheapClaimsPerRevenueDollar
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: The economic content of the claim-share mechanism is how heavily capital replacement and interest weigh on the business's scale of operations, and revenue is the correct scale measure because it is always positive; cheap firms carrying light fixed claims per dollar of revenue retain the flexibility to survive and re-rate.

considered.name: HighYieldGateUnencumberedProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), ADD(dp, xint)), sale), 2)))

considered.name: CheapUnencumberedAndGrowing
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2)), GROWTH(SUB(revt, cogs), 1))))
