considered.name: CheapSelfFundedEquityBase
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), ib), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), sale), 2))))

considered.name: CheapEquityDearToCreditors
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(xint, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 2))))

considered.name: CheapWithImprovingCreditTerms
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xint, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), 2))))

considered.name: CheapWithLongDatedObligations
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 2))))

considered.name: CheapNetCashAccretion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), sale), 2)))

considered.name: CheapBurdenAtOwnHistoricalLow
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 5))))

considered.name: CheapClaimsMeetStableProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dp, xint), sale), 2), WINSOR(VOL(RATIO(oibdp, sale), 5), 2)))))

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapWithOverheadRestructuring
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xsga, sale), 1), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms are cheap because the market expects their cost base to overwhelm their revenue; when overhead per dollar of sales actually falls, management has demonstrated it can restructure, and the operating leverage released flows to equity before analysts revise their fixed-cost assumptions.

considered.name: CheapChronicSelfFunding
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, DELTA(ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), ceq), 1)), sale)), 0.5), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: What distinguishes a mispriced cheap firm from a value trap is not whether it avoided outside capital last year but whether it has done so repeatedly: a firm that has generated earnings in excess of its capital growth in most of the past five years has a business model that funds itself, whereas an occasional good year tells the market nothing.

Free capital generation is defined as one accounting quantity, earnings minus the growth in total invested capital, and the yearly flag is an industry-relative median rank so the five-year count spans 0 to 5 with real dispersion.

considered.name: CheapSelfFundedDistributableProfit
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), ADD(dp, xint)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), sale), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: The profit an equity holder in a cheap firm can actually count on is gross profit less what capital replacement and lenders take, less whatever new borrowing was required to keep the business running; when that residual is large relative to revenue, the discount is unjustified regardless of how the accounting earnings look.
considered.reasoning: The archive's two previous level-plus-flow fusions diluted (alpha 1.3% and 0.9%) because they averaged the *ranks* of two channels, letting each leg's noise offset the other; here the level and the flow are combined inside one accounting expression, so the composite is a single economic quantity — self-funded distributable profit — with one positive deflator. It targets the two ingredients that separately deliver the archive's best alpha (3.4%) and best slope (4.75).

considered.name: CheapPayoutPerOperatingCost
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(dvc, 0), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, cash paid to shareholders net of new borrowing measures genuine surplus, and the right scale for that surplus is the firm's operating cost base — the recurring outlay the business must fund each year — because that is what determines whether the surplus is material to the enterprise.

Total operating cost is strictly positive for every operating firm, which eliminates the inversion whereby negative-gross-profit firms receive favourable scores, and it is an economically meaningful scale rather than an arbitrary positive number.

considered.name: CheapLeveredWithNearTermMaturities
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)), 0.3)), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
considered.hypothesis: Holding the amount of debt fixed, the share of it that matures within the year determines whether a cheap firm controls its own timetable; those funded long can let operating profit be recognized, while those with a large current tranche must refinance into the same adverse conditions that produced the discount.

considered.hypothesis: The complete measure of what a cheap firm returns to its capital providers is earnings less the growth in book equity — which captures dividends and repurchases together while netting out equity issuance — less any increase in debt; when that total is large, the firm is shrinking outside claims of every type out of current profit, and the equity holder's share compounds while the price stays depressed.

considered.name: LowReplacementValueDeleveraging

considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, the cash actually delivered to shareholders — dividends plus repurchases net of any equity issued, which is exactly earnings minus the growth in book equity — is the credible signal that reported profit is real and surplus to the firm's needs, and the depressed price fails to capitalize it.

considered.hypothesis: The equity of a cheap, levered firm behaves like an option on the enterprise, so a given dollar of capital returned or debt retired shifts proportionally more value to shareholders there than in an unlevered firm where the equity already owns the whole surplus.

considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), IND_ZSCORE(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(ceq, 1)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga))), IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(cogs, xsga))))))

considered.name: ProfitableCheapCapitalReturn
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, sale)), 0.5)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(ceq, 1)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga)), 2)))
considered.hypothesis: Capital handed back by a business that earns an above-median operating margin is surplus generated by trade, whereas the same capital returned by a sub-margin business is proceeds of shrinkage — asset sales, inventory run-down, or under-investment — so profitability determines whether disgorgement by a cheap firm is evidence of hidden strength or of managed decline.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the intersection of two collinear price-scaled gates with a condition drawn from the other theme entirely — operating margin — restoring an explicit profitability leg to a family that has drifted toward pure financing flows, and it is exactly the discrimination the archive's leading signal cannot make. The margin screen at the industry median leaves roughly 30% of firms scored, comparable to the accepted claim-lightness variant, so portfolio breadth is preserved.

considered.name: LeveredRevenueCheapSustainedReturn
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)), 0.5)), IND_ZSCORE(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(ceq, 1)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga)), 2), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: Where the equity of a discounted firm is effectively a residual option on the enterprise, a sustained multi-year policy of returning capital to shareholders and creditors shifts proportionally more value to equity than the same policy at an unlevered firm, because each dollar of claim extinguished raises the probability that the equity finishes in the money.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the data-handling check for a consolidation of three separately validated elements — the sales-to-price gate (alpha 3.7%, fmb 5.57), the leverage condition that was accepted as a genuine economic amplifier (alpha 3.5%, fmb 4.94), and three-year averaging (Sharpe 0.24) — each of which was tested in isolation so the combination is interpretable rather than exploratory. The leverage screen is the one condition with a mechanism explaining *why* the effect should be larger rather than merely where it is measured.

considered.name: TwoSidedCapitalReturnExpectations
considered.expression: MUL(SUB(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.6), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), 0.6)), IND_ZSCORE(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(ceq, 1)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(cogs, xsga)), 2), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: The mispricing is the disagreement between what price implies and what capital flows reveal: cheap firms that persistently return capital are stronger than their price admits, and expensive firms that persistently absorb outside capital are weaker than their price assumes, so the two corners belong in the same signal with opposite weights.
considered.reasoning: The state variable takes the values +1, 0 and −1 across the cheap, middle and expensive thirds and multiplies the capital-return z-score, so the score is highest for cheap disgorgers and lowest for expensive absorbers — which fixes the sign inconsistency of the previous version and, more importantly, makes the construction a true interaction term rather than a gated single-state effect. It is the one specification that tests the project's central claim directly, that profitability-type evidence flips its return implication with the valuation state instead of merely being layered onto it.

critic_notes.rationale: This is a direct rediscovery of the well-documented gross-profitability-plus-value composite (Novy-Marx 2013 combined with HML / Asness-Frazzini "quality at a reasonable price"), and multiplying two uniform [0,1] ranks is dominated by their average, so the claimed pure-interaction content is largely illusory.

The INDICATOR gate assigns roughly half the sample an exact value of zero, which is not "off" but is instead placed above every profitable firm with negative earnings yield — degenerate breakpoints and a ranking that contradicts the stated distress story.

Since rank(P/B) is monotonically the complement of rank(B/M), this difference of ranks is exactly an equal-weighted additive value+profitability composite, so the "disagreement measure, not a relabeled value or quality score" reasoning is internally false and the signal duplicates proposal 1.

Conditioning value on the five-year slope of ROA rather than its level is a defensible value-trap-versus-recovery distinction that is not a standard published anomaly, though the rank-product form again behaves mostly additively and the slow-moving trend may dilute the effect.

Gross-profits-to-enterprise-value is itself a published anomaly (Novy-Marx 2013), the raw unranked ratio will dominate the [0,1] margin-rank multiplier so the "interaction" is cosmetic, and negative or near-zero enterprise values will produce sign-flipping outliers.

Internally consistent (product of two positively oriented ranks with a correctly negative expected sign) and usefully aimed at the short leg, but note that price-to-sales deflated by margin is approximately price-to-earnings, so it risks partially recovering the classic earnings-yield effect.

The gated geometry is internally consistent and the liability-side profit-coverage leg is a genuine addition beyond RMW, but oibdp/(dltt+dlc+xint) has an unstable near-zero denominator for low-leverage firms that will likely dominate the z-score and needs explicit winsorization or a leverage floor, and the underlying idea sits close to the published distress/value-trap literature.

(oancf − ib)/at is the negative of total accruals, so the signal is the Sloan (1996) accruals anomaly restricted to high book-to-market firms — a well-documented interaction (accruals are strongest in value/low-quality segments) rather than a new cross-theme mechanism.

A one-year change in ROA applied inside a high book-to-market gate is essentially the ΔROA component of Piotroski's (2000) F-score strategy, which was published precisely as fundamental-signal screening within value stocks, so this is a rediscovery rather than a repair.

The expression, gate direction, and positive expected sign are mutually consistent and the glamour-side mirror is a legitimate diagnostic that isolates where the value–profitability interaction is generated, though it is a symmetric variant of a Piotroski-style ΔROA screen and its incremental content over the cheap-side version may be thin.

Holding profitability high and letting log book-to-market generate the spread reduces the signal to the classic value effect on a profitable subsample — the proposal itself concedes it retains HML exposure, so it is near-guaranteed to be absorbed by FF5 and is too trivial a construction to be worth a slot.

This combines two well-published anomalies — intangible/R&D-adjusted book-to-market (Park; Eisfeldt-Kim-Papanikolaou) and gross profitability (Novy-Marx) — and the claim that the restated valuation leg cannot be absorbed by HML is unsupported since cumulative-R&D-adjusted B/M is very highly correlated with raw B/M for the large majority of firms where COALESCE sets R&D to zero.

This is a cosmetic variant of the archived DeepValueTrapScreen — same gate-times-profitability geometry, same grading channel, with only a highly correlated cheapness proxy (EBITDA/P vs OCF/P) substituted and the threshold simultaneously moved from 0.7 to 0.6, so it neither isolates one design choice nor introduces a new economic mechanism.

Still the same template as the archived winner, but replacing equity-based cheapness with a strictly-positive enterprise-yield gate addresses a genuine confound (leverage) that all prior archive gates share, and the expression cleanly matches the stated hypothesis.

The level-vs-persistence question is worth asking, but every other archive use of INDICATOR takes a cross-sectional rank/quantile as its second argument, so INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp,at), 0.02) is likely to be read as a ~2nd-percentile threshold and return 1 for nearly all firms, making TS_SUM a near-constant with almost no cross-sectional dispersion.

Gating on sales-to-price and then sorting on operating margin selects almost exactly the high-earnings-yield firms, so the long leg is a rediscovery of the E/P anomaly dressed as a two-channel interaction, and the archive already found the closely related P/S-times-margin construction unproductive.

The dividend-yield gate is a genuinely fresh valuation channel, but the grading term (oiadp − dvc)/at is numerically dominated by ROA since dvc/at is typically an order of magnitude smaller, so the expression does not actually measure payout coverage as the hypothesis claims and reduces to yield-gated profitability.

Capital intensity of profits is a legitimately novel and plausibly FF5-orthogonal grading channel, but dp/oibdp flips sign whenever operating profit is negative — common among cheap value firms and far more than 2% of the gated sample — so NEG(WINSOR(...)) will systematically award top scores to loss-making firms, contradicting the stated mechanism.

A defensible orthogonal-leg fusion of the archive's two partial successes with a broader gross-profit-to-price gate, but it is fundamentally an additive recombination of already-tested components rather than a new mechanism, and SUMRANK of a coarse 0–5 persistence count with a continuous burden ratio risks the discrete leg dominating the composite ordering.

This is explicitly a single-operator construction variant of archived CheapWithLowCapitalConsumption (indicator swapped for continuous rank) with no new economic content, exactly the cosmetic re-parameterization the objective warns against.

A well-diagnosed repair that puts the unstable leverage quantity in the numerator over a near-always-positive denominator, though "cheap plus low financial-distress burden" is close to the well-worn safe-value/Piotroski-leverage screen and only modestly extends the archive's burden-ratio family.

The net-cash-to-market-cap valuation channel is genuinely distinct from every book-, earnings-, and cash-flow-yield gate in the archive, and the profitability interaction is economically necessary rather than decorative since net-cash cheapness is dominated by cash-burning firms; the main risk is that the long leg concentrates in small, illiquid, cash-rich names.

The diagnosis (strong alpha, flat slope) is honest and the added profitability leg is substantive rather than cosmetic, but averaging a second rank into the archive's best-alpha signal is as likely to dilute that alpha as to supply a slope, and payout-sustainability screens on high-yield stocks are close to established dividend-safety practice.

Value combined with R&D intensity is a direct rediscovery of the well-published R&D-to-market / intangible-adjusted-value anomaly (Chan-Lakonishok-Sougiannis, Eisfeldt et al.), and the COALESCE-to-zero convention creates a large mass point so the signal effectively reduces to "cheap R&D reporters vs. everyone else."

Economically coherent and sign-consistent, but (GP−dp−xint)/GP is just 1 minus the sum of the two already-archived burden ratios inside the identical cheap gate, so it is closer to a re-parameterization than a new mechanism — and the claim that it is "free of sign flips" is wrong, since firms with negative gross profit get a large positive (good) score from the same deductions.

Treating dividends as a prior "claim" that destroys equity value is economically incoherent (dividends accrue to the equity holder, and the archived dividend result was conditional on a high-yield gate, not a generic burden), and the four-term aggregate is explicitly assembled by sign-fitting to in-sample archive t-stats rather than from a prior.

Level-plus-flow of claims on gross profit is a defensible pairing with a correct diagnosis of why the gen-3 SUMRANK fusion failed, though it remains a recombination of two archived grading channels under the same gate and inherits their negative-gross-profit denominator instability.

This is essentially gross-profit-to-price (Novy-Marx's valuation-ratio version of gross profitability) with depreciation and interest netted out — a known published value ratio, not a cross-theme interaction, and it abandons the interaction mandate entirely to test a single univariate yield.

A genuine mechanism-location test that runs the validated burden channel in the opposite valuation state with an internally consistent expected sign and a construction directly comparable to the cheap-gate signals, so either outcome is informative about whether the effect is distress-specific.

Pairing the net-cash gate (strong FMB, weak alpha) with the capital-consumption channel (weak FMB, reliable alpha) is a sensible attempt to reconcile the two evidence types, but the grading leg is monotone-equivalent to an archived one, and the stated microcap fix is doubtful since dp/GP proxies asset intensity rather than cash burn and inverts for negative-gross-profit firms.

A coherent generalization of the archive's best flow signal into a net-payout-to-capital measure, but it is close to the known net-external-financing anomaly, it retains the negative-gross-profit denominator inversion the proposal set elsewhere admits is a defect, and it enters dvc with the opposite sign to the two archived dividend-gated signals without reconciling that tension.

This is a pure horizon-tuning variant of CheapDeleveragingFromProfits — one operator argument changed — which is exactly the cosmetic re-parameterization the objective asks researchers to avoid, and its diagnostic value does not justify a full evaluation slot.

Value-gated net share issuance is a thin wrapper on the well-documented net-stock-issuance/composite-issuance anomaly, and the construction is mechanically flawed because raw DELTA(csho) is contaminated by splits and stock dividends and the gross-profit denominator flips sign for loss-making cheap firms.

The denominator swap is motivated by a real and correctly diagnosed inversion in the gross-profit-scaled burden family, making it a legitimate robustness test rather than a cosmetic tweak, though the grading leg reduces to a fairly standard capital-intensity/leverage measure and the expected incremental insight is modest.

The stated mechanism is undermined by the arithmetic: raw operating earnings yield has an order of magnitude more cross-sectional dispersion than the effective borrowing rate, so the signal will be dominated by plain E/P — a canonical value anomaly — contradicting the claim that neither leg carries the signal, and zero-debt firms make the promised "full coverage" false.

A sensible test of whether the dividend gate's reliable alphas come from payout safety or general earning power, and the revenue scaling avoids the negative-denominator problem, but the archived dividend-gated signals all show strong alphas with null Fama-MacBeth slopes, so this likely reinherits a gate-driven, grading-leg-independent result.

The conditioning leg is essentially the published net-external-financing / composite-issuance anomaly (Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan, Daniel-Titman) and, within this archive, a mechanical dollar sum of the two already-tested legs (CheapDeleveragingFromProfits and CheapSelfFundedEquityBase) that debt flows will numerically dominate, so it is closer to a repackaging than a new mechanism.

This is a denominator swap on the immediately preceding proposal, and deflating the financing flow by market cap puts 1/price in both the gate and the signal, so any measured edge is partly a mechanical value/size repackaging rather than evidence about the financing channel.

The timing-of-credit-repricing channel is a legitimate extension of the archive's cross-market idea, but DELTA(xint/debt) falls mechanically when debt is raised late in the fiscal year, so the computed quantity is heavily contaminated by debt issuance — the very thing the archive's deleveraging signal treats with the opposite sign.

A sign-flipped gate on the same construction as proposal 1, testing what is already well documented — that issuance and asset-growth/external-finance effects are concentrated in high-multiple firms — and it overlaps heavily with FF5's CMA and the share-issuance anomaly.

Besides being a re-run of the already-diluted level-plus-flow fusion with a different deflator, the flow leg drops COALESCE(dvc,0) so DELTA(ceq)-ib mixes payout into "external finance abstinence," directly contradicting the reconciliation the same batch used to justify including dividends.

Debt maturity structure is a genuinely distinct, FF5-orthogonal channel not represented anywhere in the archive, though the ratio is unstable for firms with trivial total debt (all-current-maturity micro-balances score as extreme rollover risk) and the WINSOR on an already-bounded ratio is inert, so an interaction with leverage level would sharpen it.

The persistence-count statistic is a genuinely different construction, but the underlying yearly quantity (earnings minus growth in invested capital) is essentially negative net external financing — a well-documented published anomaly and, up to the dividend term, the same channel already run twice in the archive (CheapSelfFundedEquityBase, CheapProfitFundedDisgorgement), so the incremental information is modest.

This is the archive's top signal (CheapProfitFundedDisgorgement) with two simultaneous changes — deflator and cheapness gate — so it is both a near-duplicate and a confounded robustness test that cannot attribute any difference to the claimed denominator repair.

Fusing the level (gross profit net of depreciation and interest) and the flow (debt issuance) inside one revenue-deflated accounting quantity is a substantively different construction from the earlier rank-averaged composites, though subtracting new borrowing from a "distributable profit" measure inverts the standard FCFE treatment of net borrowing and makes the quantity a hybrid of profitability and financing rather than a clean earning-power measure.

The stated mechanism is maturity structure, but dlc/sale is dominated by the level of short-term borrowing relative to firm scale — i.e., a leverage measure — so the expression does not compute the timing-of-obligations construct the hypothesis claims and the asserted orthogonality to size-of-obligations is contradicted by its own construction.

Cash-to-assets as a return predictor is a well-established published anomaly (Palazzo 2012 and the corporate-cash-holdings literature), and gating it on a cheapness rank is a trivial one-step interaction that also overlaps the archived NetCashValueWithProfit gate.

This is the archived CheapDeleveragingFromProfits expression with the gate threshold moved from 0.6 to 0.8 — a pure parameter tweak of the kind the objective explicitly discourages, and one that will mechanically shrink coverage and destabilize portfolio composition.

A legitimate and interpretable ablation of the archive's best performer (dropping the creditor term), though it sits close to the well-known net-payout/net-share-issuance anomaly and overlaps materially with CheapSelfFundedEquityBase, so the incremental information is the deflator-and-gate combination rather than the underlying construct.

This is CheapDeleveragingFromProfits with the denominator swapped from gross profit to cogs+xsga — same gate, same numerator, same NEG and winsorization — which is precisely the kind of cosmetic deflator variant the objective warns against, and the "decomposition" framing does not make a one-term denominator change a new mechanism.

Rescaling the winner's payload by total assets is another deflator swap rather than a new economic condition, and in that form ib−Δceq−Δdebt over assets is close to the published net-external-financing/free-cash-flow anomaly; the coverage argument is also weak since archive signals using cogs+xsga already reach 0.109 versus ~0.13 for asset-scaled ones.

The stated diagnostic ("does averaging strengthen the 3.5%/t=2.62 one-year result?") is not identified by this expression because it changes both the deflator (at instead of cogs+xsga) and the horizon simultaneously, so any difference cannot be attributed to smoothing, and absent that the proposal reduces to a routine MA(3) smoothing variant.

The option-on-the-enterprise argument is a genuine second economic condition rather than a threshold tweak, but the double gate leaves ~75% of the cross-section at exactly zero and the Δdebt term in the payload is mechanically correlated with the leverage screen, so portfolio stability and interpretation both need close scrutiny.

Substituting a flow-based cheapness gate for the balance-sheet gate is a defensible test of whether the mechanism requires book-value cheapness specifically, and it is not a rediscovery, though it remains a single-component swap and the prior sales-to-price gated signal in the archive performed poorly, tempering the prior.

A defensible but purely mechanical merge of two already-tested gen-8 variants whose parents perform almost identically, so the incremental information is small, and the payload — (ib − Δceq − Δdebt), i.e. net distributions to all claimants — remains a close relative of the published net-external-financing/total-payout anomaly conditioned on value, which limits novelty even if the test is worth one run.

Intersecting two highly correlated market-cap-scaled cheapness gates is a conditioning/threshold tweak rather than a new economic mechanism, and because sales/P and B/P share the same denominator the intersection will largely reproduce either parent while further thinning an already coverage-constrained (0.109) sample.

This is a data-handling robustness check on the deflator, not a cross-theme signal; the coverage gain over the parent is modest (~0.109 → ~0.14 at best), and COALESCE(xsga,0) silently changes the deflator's economic meaning across reporting regimes, so a "surviving" result is as likely to reflect deflator heterogeneity as genuine breadth.

The sustainability condition is economically coherent and gating rather than rank-averaging is the right response to the earlier SUMRANK dilution, but stacking a second 0.5 gate on top of a 0.6 gate within an already sparse sample risks unstable extreme portfolios, so coverage and turnover diagnostics must be checked before crediting any alpha improvement.

This is the one proposal that asks a genuine structural question — whether the shareholder-payout and debt-retirement legs are additive or complementary — and the MIN construction is not reproducible by the existing sum, so the result is informative regardless of sign; it is distinct from the earlier CheapCashBackedCapitalReturn, which paired the combined flow with operating cash flow instead.

The stated sign contradicts the expression: the payload is high when a firm *returns* capital and low when it *absorbs* it, so the hypothesis ("capital absorbers underperform") implies a positive slope, not the declared negative one, and beyond this inconsistency the design is a sign-flipped gate on an already-tested payload.
